slides.title: When do we use them?
slides.text:
We use them when a person does something **to** or **for** themselves.

I looked at **myself** in the mirror.
The cat washed **itself**.

slides.title: Match the person
slides.text:
I → **myself**
he → **himself**
she → **herself**
it → **itself**

**Sara** cut **herself**.
**Ali** hurt **himself**.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find **who** did the action.
2. Is it a boy, a girl, a thing, or many people?
3. Pick the -self word that matches.

The sentence that tells who did it is your proof.

sentences.t: Now his knee has a bandage.

example.explain: Sentence 1 tells us **Omar** fell. Omar is a boy, so he hurt **himself**.

together.passage: Lama is nine years old. Today she baked a cake. Nobody helped her. She made it all by ___.
together.hint: Who made the cake? Is that a boy, a girl or many people?
together.good: Yes! Lama made the cake alone, so she made it by **herself**.

evidence.stem: The answer was: herself. Tap 2 sentences that show who baked and that she did it alone.
evidence.wrong: This sentence tells about Lama, but not about the baking. Find who baked and who helped.

checks.why: The person is **I**, so we use **myself**.

checks.passage: The dog scratched ___ behind the ear.
checks.why: The dog is an animal, so we use **itself**.
**Badr** is a boy, so he dressed **himself**.

again.title: The mirror trick
again.text: Think of a mirror. The person does the action and **sees themselves**. Use a -self word.
again.example:
Huda looks in the mirror. She sees **herself**.

The boys look in the mirror. They see **themselves**.

slides.title: One or many
slides.text:
One person: **myself**, **yourself**, **himself**, **herself**, **itself**

Many people: **ourselves**, **yourselves**, **themselves**

For many, the ending is **-selves**.

slides.title: Words that do not exist
slides.text:
These are **not** English words:

✘ hisself → ✔ **himself**
✘ theirselves → ✔ **themselves**
✘ ourself → ✔ **ourselves**

slides.title: By myself
slides.text:
**by + -self** means **alone**, with no help.

I walked home **by myself**.
The children set up the tent **by themselves**.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find who did the action.
2. Count: one person or more than one?
3. Look for clues that they acted **alone** or on **themselves**.

The sentences that name the people and show what they did are your proof.

sentences.t: We dug the soil and watered the seeds by ourselves.

example.explain:
**Our class** and **we** mean many people, so we use **ourselves**.

The teacher only watched, which shows the class did it **alone**.

together.passage: Mom was tired after a long day at work. Her twin sons, Saad and Majed, wanted to help. They washed the dishes and cleaned the kitchen by ___. Nobody asked them to do it. When Mom came home, she smiled and said, "You should be proud of yourselves!"
together.hint: How many boys cleaned? Which -self words are real English words?
together.good: Yes! Two boys did the work alone, so: **by themselves**.

sentences: Mom was tired after a long day at work.
Her twin sons, Saad and Majed, wanted to help.
They washed the dishes and cleaned the kitchen by ___.
Nobody asked them to do it.
When Mom came home, she smiled and said, "You should be proud of yourselves!"
evidence.stem: The answer was: themselves. Tap 2 sentences that show who did the work and that they did it alone.
evidence.wrong: This sentence is about Mom, not about who cleaned. Find the sentences about the twins.

checks.passage: You and Fahad can serve ___ some juice.
checks.why: **You and Fahad** are two people, so we use **yourselves**.

checks.passage: My grandfather taught hisself to read when he was young.
checks.why: **hisself** is not an English word. It should be **himself**.

checks.passage: My sister and I made breakfast by ___.
checks.why: **My sister and I** = we, so the word is **ourselves**.

again.title: Swap and check
again.text: Change the people to one simple word: I, he, she, it, we, you, they. Then add the ending.
again.example:
The players → **they** → **themselves**
My friends and I → **we** → **ourselves**
My aunt → **she** → **herself**

slides.title: Reflexive or object?
slides.text:
Use a **reflexive** pronoun when the subject and the object are the **same** person.

Ali taught **himself** to swim. (Ali taught Ali)

Use an **object** pronoun when they are **different**.

Ali taught **him** to swim. (Ali taught another boy)

slides.title: You or you all?
slides.text:
**yourself** = one person
**yourselves** = more than one

A teacher to one student: Be proud of **yourself**.
A teacher to the class: Be proud of **yourselves**.

slides.title: Not as a subject
slides.text:
Do not use a -self word as the subject.

✘ Hassan and **myself** went to the market.
✔ Hassan and **I** went to the market.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the subject of the sentence.
2. Ask: is the action going back to the **same** person or people?
3. Check how many people are being spoken to or about.

The sentences that show who is involved are your proof.

sentences.t: The coach spoke to Noor after the match.
"Don't blame yourself for the goal," she said.

example.explain: The coach is speaking to **one** player, Noor. Noor should not blame Noor, so the coach says **yourself**.

together.passage: Before the big race, our coach gathered the whole team together. "Do not compare yourselves to other runners," she said. "Just believe in ___ and run your best." Then she handed each of us a water bottle and wished us luck. Moments later, the starting whistle blew.
together.hint: Is the coach speaking to one runner or to the whole team?
together.good: Yes! She is speaking to the **whole team**, and the runners should believe in themselves: **yourselves**.

sentences: Before the big race, our coach gathered the whole team together.
"Do not compare yourselves to other runners," she said.
"Just believe in ___ and run your best."
Then she handed each of us a water bottle and wished us luck.
Moments later, the starting whistle blew.
evidence.stem: The answer was: yourselves. Tap 2 sentences that show she is speaking to more than one person.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not show who the coach is talking to. Find the clues about the whole team.

checks.passage: Reem looked at the photo of her cousin and smiled at ___.
checks.why: Reem smiled at her **cousin**, a different person. So we use the object pronoun **her**.

checks.passage: ___ and my brother cleaned the yard.
checks.why: This is the subject of the sentence, so we use **I**, not myself.

checks.passage: The new robot can switch ___ off when the battery is low.
checks.why: The robot switches **the robot** off: same subject and object, so **itself**.

again.title: Who gets the action?
again.text:
Draw an arrow from the doer to the person who **receives** the action.

Arrow comes back to the doer? Use **-self**.
Arrow goes to someone else? Use **me, him, her, them**.
again.example:
Sami washed **himself**. (arrow comes back)
Sami washed **him**. (arrow goes to another boy)

slides.title: Reflexive pronouns
slides.text:
A **reflexive** pronoun is the **object** of the verb or a preposition. It refers back to the subject, and the sentence needs it.

She taught **herself** to code.
(Remove it: 'She taught to code.' ✘)

slides.title: Intensive pronouns
slides.text:
An **intensive** pronoun uses the same words, but only adds **emphasis**. The sentence works without it.

The principal **herself** greeted us.
(Remove it: 'The principal greeted us.' ✔)

slides.title: Overusing myself
slides.text:
Some people use **myself** to sound formal. It is incorrect when there is no 'I' doing the action.

✘ Please send your questions to Ms Noura or **myself**.
✔ Please send your questions to Ms Noura or **me**.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
Use the **removal test** on each sentence.

1. Cover the -self word.
2. Does the sentence still make sense?
3. Yes → intensive (emphasis). No → reflexive (needed as an object).

Sentences that fail the test prove the pronoun is reflexive.

sentences.t: The scientist herself checked every result.
She reminded herself to stay patient.

example.explain:
Remove **herself** from sentence 1: 'The scientist checked every result.' It works, so it is **intensive**.

Remove **herself** from sentence 2: 'She reminded to stay patient.' It fails, so it is **reflexive**.

together.passage: When the new community centre opened in our town, the mayor himself cut the ribbon. The building had been designed by a young architect who had taught herself to draw as a child. She told the crowd that the design itself came from the shapes of old mud-brick houses. Volunteers had painted the walls themselves over three weekends. After the speeches, visitors helped themselves to dates and coffee in the courtyard.
together.stem: Which phrase uses a reflexive pronoun as the OBJECT of the verb?
options: the mayor himself cut the ribbon
together.hint: Cover the -self word in each choice. Which one no longer makes sense?
together.good: Yes! 'Visitors helped to dates' makes no sense, so **themselves** is a needed object: it is reflexive.

sentences: When the new community centre opened in our town, the mayor himself cut the ribbon.
The building had been designed by a young architect who had taught herself to draw as a child.
She told the crowd that the design itself came from the shapes of old mud-brick houses.
Volunteers had painted the walls themselves over three weekends.
After the speeches, visitors helped themselves to dates and coffee in the courtyard.
evidence.stem: The answer was: visitors helped themselves. Tap 2 sentences where the -self word is a needed object (the removal test fails).
evidence.wrong: Cover the -self word here and the sentence still works, so it only adds emphasis. Find one that fails the test.

checks.passage: If you have any questions about the trip, please ask Mr Khalid or ___.
checks.why: The writer is not doing an action to himself, so the object pronoun **me** is correct.

checks.passage: The students themselves chose the theme for the school festival.
checks.stem: What does 'themselves' do in this sentence?
options: It is the subject of the sentence.
It shows the students did something to themselves.
It adds emphasis and could be removed.
checks.why: 'The students chose the theme' still works, so **themselves** is intensive. It adds emphasis.

checks.passage: After the long hike, the travellers allowed ___ a short rest.
checks.why: The travellers allowed **the travellers** a rest. Same subject and object, so: **themselves**.

again.title: Cover it up
again.text:
Put your finger over the -self word and read again.

Still fine? It is just for **emphasis**.
Broken? It is a **reflexive** object, and the sentence needs it.
again.example:
I made the bread **myself**. → 'I made the bread.' Still fine: **emphasis**.

I burned **myself**. → 'I burned.' Broken: **reflexive**.
